This message comes from Angie. Angie has been helping homeowners find skilled
pros to get their home projects done well for over 30 years. For everything from minor repairs
to major remodels, find reviews, pricing, and booking at Angie.com or on the Angie app.
This is NPR News Now. The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton. A bystander who intervened in yesterday's attack
at a school in Oregon is being hailed as a hero. The man who's a father of two students at Silver
Rail Elementary School shot and killed the 16-year-old gunman. As NPR's Jacqueline Diaz reports,
this kind of armed intervention by a civilian doesn't happen often.
James Stensley is co-founder of the Violence Prevention Project. It's a group that studies
incidents of public violence. He and his colleagues tracked every homicide at K-12
schools in the U.S. since 2000. Across 400 incidents, they found no cases of a civilian
shooting to stop an attacker. What we usually see is when a school shooting is stopped before the
police get there, it's almost always by someone with no gun. And it's usually a teacher, custodian,
or even a student. Jacqueline Diaz, NPR News. A new congressional report says President Trump's
stock holdings in pharmaceutical companies have grown dramatically. NPR's Sydney Lupkin reports.
Minority members on the Joint Economic Committee issued a report Friday that says the president's
stock holdings in pharmaceutical companies were worth as much as $56.2 million in 2025. That's up
from as much as $1.7 million in 2024. The report is based on the president's annual financial
disclosures. Those documents offer ranges but not exact dollar amounts for each stock. The report
shows significant increases in the president's holdings in Johnson & Johnson, Merck, Eli Lilly,
and others. The president's wealth overall has grown significantly in his second term,
NPR reporting has found. Sydney Lupkin, NPR News. Tech giant Anthropik says next month it will
formalize new rules governing how people treat its AI chatbot. As NPR's Windsor Johnston reports,
the policy is sparking debate over artificial intelligence and the concept of feelings.
Starting November 12th, Anthropik will explicitly prohibit extreme sustained abuse toward Claude,
but the move is raising questions about why a chatbot needs protection from cruelty when
there's no clear evidence it can feel. Jeff Sebo is the director of the Center for Mind
Ethics and Policy at NYU. This concern for AI consciousness and welfare is not coming from a
place of certainty or confidence that the models have feelings and emotions but is instead coming
from curiosity and open-mindedness. Sebo warns that certainty in either direction carries risks,
encouraging unhealthy attachments to chatbots or overlooking the possibility of AI suffering.
Windsor Johnston, NPR News. Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh isn't signaling what the
Fed will do about interest rates and its upcoming meetings, but stubbornly high inflation is expected
to lead the Fed to raise its key interest rate in the coming months after a rate hike in September.
Stocks closed lower on Wall Street today as more drops for big tech companies weighed down the
market. This is NPR News from Washington. The U.S. is attempting to revive three
shuttered nuclear plants to meet growing demand, especially from data centers.
It's unprecedented. No nuclear reactor is resumed generating electricity after being decommissioned.
The federal government is lending up to $4.4 billion to restart plants in Michigan,
Pennsylvania, and Iowa. Demonstrators in France are hoping for an alliance between student
protesters and the Yellow Vest movement that mobilized against high gas prices in the
government eight years ago. And Pierre's Eleanor Beardsley reports an economic crisis could bring
the movements together in what's being billed as a day of anger. The French interior minister says
90 protest marches and 500 separate actions are planned across the country. Social media posts
indicate that there could be an alliance between the students who are protesting dilapidated
facilities, overcrowded classrooms and a lack of teachers, and a reconstituted Yellow Vest movement
of angry white working class voters. Everyone is demanding more government spending and protections
against rising energy prices. But with France mired in debt and with record high borrowing costs,
the government has little room to maneuver. Meanwhile, stores in some cities are boarding
up their windows ahead of tomorrow's protests. Eleanor Beardsley, NPR News, Paris.
The NBA is restricting certain types of betting following scandals that led to arrests of current
and former NBA figures. It includes bets on which player records the first stat of a game and the
outcome of the opening tip-off. The league also requires players, coaches, and staff to attend
in-person training on sports betting rules. This is NPR News.

U.S. government lends up to $4.4 billion to restart three shuttered nuclear plants in Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Iowa
